name: Small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcaemic type
aliases: hypercalcaemic small cell carcinoma of the ovary
ovarian small cell carcinoma of hypercalcaemic type

reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Female Genital Tumours / Berek and Hacker's Gynecologic Oncology
clinicalPearls: This is a rare, highly aggressive ovarian malignancy that characteristically affects adolescents and young women rather than older adults
About two-thirds of patients have paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia, which may cause fatigue, nausea, constipation, polyuria, and confusion and can be the presenting clue
Despite the historical name, it is not of neuroendocrine origin; it is now defined by loss of the chromatin-remodelling protein SMARCA4 (BRG1)
It shares molecular features with malignant rhabdoid tumours, and some cases are associated with germline SMARCA4 variants, so family history and genetic assessment matter
Tumours are usually large and unilateral at diagnosis and frequently present at an advanced stage with extra-ovarian spread
Diagnosis rests on histology with immunohistochemistry demonstrating loss of SMARCA4 (BRG1) expression, distinguishing it from other small round cell tumours

Management is delivered by a gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team and combines tumour-directed surgery with aggressive chemotherapy, and the hypercalcaemia typically resolves as the tumour is controlled
reference.pathophysiology: Small cell carcinoma of the ovary of hypercalcaemic type is a chromatin-remodelling-driven malignancy defined by inactivation of SMARCA4, the gene encoding BRG1, a core ATPase subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling complex. Loss of this subunit disrupts the complex's control of gene expression and differentiation, driving an undifferentiated, highly proliferative tumour that resembles malignant rhabdoid tumours molecularly. The paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia is attributed to tumour production of parathyroid hormone-related protein, which promotes bone resorption and renal calcium retention independent of bony metastasis. A subset of patients carry germline SMARCA4 variants, linking the tumour to an inherited rhabdoid tumour predisposition.
additionalDifferentials: Adult granulosa cell tumour and other sex cord-stromal tumours
Dysgerminoma and other malignant germ cell tumours
Small cell carcinoma of pulmonary type involving the ovary
Metastatic small round blue cell tumours (e.g. lymphoma, neuroblastoma)
additionalInvestigations: Histopathology with immunohistochemistry showing loss of SMARCA4 (BRG1) expression
Serum corrected calcium and parathyroid hormone-related protein assessment
Cross-sectional imaging of the abdomen, pelvis, and chest for staging
Serum tumour markers to help exclude germ cell and epithelial tumours
Germline SMARCA4 genetic testing and genetic counselling
Baseline renal function and electrocardiography in the context of hypercalcaemia
redFlags: Severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia with dehydration, arrhythmia, or altered consciousness requiring urgent correction
A rapidly enlarging pelvic or abdominal mass with constitutional symptoms
Evidence of advanced-stage disease with extra-ovarian spread
A young patient with an ovarian mass and unexplained hypercalcaemia
reference.prognosis: The tumour is aggressive and carries a poor prognosis overall, particularly when it presents at an advanced stage, though outcomes are better for early-stage disease treated with multimodal therapy. Younger age and higher stage generally portend a worse outcome, and relapse is common.
pitfalls: Assuming ovarian cancer is a disease of older women and discounting it in a young patient
Attributing hypercalcaemia to bony metastases rather than recognising a paraneoplastic mechanism
Misclassifying the tumour as a germ cell or sex cord-stromal neoplasm without SMARCA4 immunohistochemistry
Overlooking the possibility of a germline SMARCA4 variant and omitting genetic referral
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Female Genital Tumours
management: Refer promptly to a gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team given the rarity and aggressiveness of SCCOHT
For early-stage, resectable disease, perform primary cytoreductive surgery with formal staging followed by adjuvant multi-agent platinum-based chemotherapy
For advanced or bulky disease, consider neoadjuvant chemotherapy to allow interval cytoreductive surgery, followed by further adjuvant chemotherapy
Consider radiotherapy to the pelvis or sites of residual or high-risk disease as an adjunct to surgery and chemotherapy
Consider high-dose chemotherapy with autologous stem cell rescue as consolidation in appropriately fit patients who respond to first-line therapy
For relapsed or refractory disease, individualise treatment, prioritise clinical trial enrolment, and select salvage regimens case by case
Consider investigational SMARCA4 or SWI-SNF-directed agents such as EZH2 inhibitors in specialist or trial settings for relapsed disease
Treat paraneoplastic hypercalcaemia with intravenous rehydration and bone-resorption inhibitors such as bisphosphonates or calcitonin, in parallel with oncological treatment
Provide supportive oncological care including antiemetics, nutritional support, and management of treatment-related toxicity throughout systemic therapy
Monitor for relapse with periodic cross-sectional imaging and serial serum corrected calcium
Monitor renal function and cardiac status in patients with significant hypercalcaemia
Arrange clinical genetics assessment and cascade testing given the association with germline SMARCA4 variants and rhabdoid tumour predisposition
Involve palliative care early for symptom control and supportive decision-making in advanced or relapsed disease
